717adbe3f5.a: Sarah believes in a great person theory of history and rejects the narrative that one or two labs will consume the entire economy. While she acknowledges the landscape is violently competitive and globally competitive, she argues that high-agency people with correct risk capital, support, and networks can change outcomes. She emphasizes that individual entrepreneurs and researchers can affect whether a competitive open-source model emerges and whether the ecosystem remains diverse rather than consolidated.
717adbe3f5.e: She Knows the 250 People Building AI. Here's What They Actually Believe.
f: Consolidation is not inevitable. High-agency entrepreneurs and researchers with proper capital, support, and networks can prevent a handful of labs from consuming the entire AI economy , even in a violently competitive landscape. Individual decision-makers matter more than structural forces.

The anxiety around AI consolidation runs deep. Many investors and observers assume that recursive self-improvement and the capital demands of frontier model development will naturally funnel power into one or two dominant labs. Sarah rejects this fatalism outright.

Her reasoning rests on what she calls a belief in the "great man and great woman theories of history." As Sarah explains in the episode , the outcome of AI development hinges not on inexorable market forces but on the people involved and their environment. Two researchers with the same code but different networks, capital sources, and support systems will end up in entirely different places.
Why the ecosystem diversity question matters now

The critical juncture is not whether open-source models exist—they already do. The question is whether a competitive Western open-source model will emerge at the frontier, one capable of competing alongside proprietary efforts from OpenAI, DeepMind, and others. This matters because it determines whether the economic and strategic benefits of AI development remain broadly distributed or collapse into a handful of organizations.

Sarah's position is that this outcome is not predetermined. Whether the ecosystem remains diverse or becomes monolithic depends on specific investments, hiring decisions, and strategic choices made by individuals right now. A researcher who gets hired by a scrappy frontier lab instead of OpenAI could change the trajectory of that lab. A founder who chooses to open-source their work instead of licensing it to a hyperscaler shapes the competitive landscape. As discussed in the episode , Sarah is tracking approximately 250 such high-agency people at the frontier of AI innovation, betting that their choices and capabilities will shape whether consolidation happens.

f799d351f3.q: How does open source model growth affect AI infrastructure demand and compute margins?
f799d351f3.a: Open source models like GLM 5.2 and Kimi shifted the token mix from expensive frontier model tokens with 80-95% inference margins toward open source alternatives. While this reduces margin dollars for frontier model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, it does not reduce overall compute demand because all tokens require identical amounts of computing resources. Open source effectively transfers margin dollars from frontier model providers directly to the AI infrastructure layer where cloud providers charge the same amount for compute, so total demand for infrastructure remains unchanged or increases due to the margin elasticity effect.
